transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-12-07 15:30 UTC. Recording start.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, really appreciate you making time — I'm Maya, I'm the AE on the account, and Derek my SE will run through the technical bits. Um, how's everyone doing?
[00:07] Priya Nair: Good, thanks. Busy quarter but excited to get this scoped out.
[00:10] Derek Salazar: Hey all, quick agenda: SOC 2/ISO posture, trust center access, RBAC/SSO, logs + SIEM export, KMS options and data residency. We'll leave time for Qs. Sound okay?
[00:20] Liam O'Rourke: Yep, that's perfect. We're primarily here to validate the controls and understand integration effort.
[00:25] Sara Mendoza: And to confirm evidence flow for our auditors — what gets pulled when.

[00:40] Maya Chen: Great. To start, Redwood's SOC 2 Type II covers hosted inference API — that's our baseline. We also provide dedicated pools and private deployment variants under the same control framework. We'll share a redacted report and the Trust Center link after this call.
[00:55] Priya Nair: Quick question — does your SOC scope include Dedicated and Private deployments or just hosted? We need to be clear for our scope mapping.
[01:05] Derek Salazar: Short answer: Type II covers our hosted managed environment and the control baseline we apply across all modes. For Dedicated and Private, we provide a controls mapping and operation playbook; some customer-run controls remain in their scope, for example, network segmentation in private/VPC. We'll walk through which controls transfer and which are shared.
[01:25] Priya Nair: Okay. Can you show how that mapping looks?
[01:30] Derek Salazar: Sure — example: logical access control — in hosted, Redwood manages identity, provisioning, and role-based access. In Dedicated we still manage the inference runtime and auditing, but the customer controls the VPC and network ACLs, so that sits with you. We'll provide a mapping doc that lines each SOC 2 control to "Redwood", "Customer", or "Shared".

[02:05] Liam O'Rourke: For SSO, we run Okta with SAML. We need SCIM provisioning and MFA enforcement. How mature is your SCIM support?
[02:15] Maya Chen: We support SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning for RBAC sync; MFA enforcement is handled by the IdP. Derek, can you give the specifics?
[02:22] Derek Salazar: Yep — we support SAML 2.0 including encrypted assertions, and SCIM v2 for user/group provisioning. Groups map to Redwood roles (admin, dev, read-only). You can also create custom roles via the Console. A note — sometimes group names in the transcript get munged if customers have unusual characters, but SCIM handles attributes like email, displayName, memberOf.
[02:43] Priya Nair: Good. We'd want to restrict a small set of service accounts and ensure audit trail for changes.
[02:48] Derek Salazar: Absolutely — we log all IAM changes, role grants, SCIM events in the audit stream. You can pull those logs via API or send to your SIEM (S3/CloudStorage or syslog) with retention controls.

[03:15] Sara Mendoza: About audit logs — retention default is 90 days right? We need 12 months for our audit. How do we get that?
[03:22] Derek Salazar: Default retention depends on plan; for enterprise we support configurable retention and export. For your case we recommend pushing daily rollups to your S3 bucket or a SIEM — we can keep raw logs longer on request, but exports are the recommended pattern. We'll include a sample lifecycle policy.
[03:40] Liam O'Rourke: Will logs contain PII? We try to avoid sending any customer data outside of our systems.
[03:46] Maya Chen: We redact customer payloads from operational logs by default; tokens and user content aren't stored in plain logs. Derek, detail on redaction?
[03:54] Derek Salazar: Right — request payloads are not logged verbatim. We log metadata: request id, model invoked, model version, token counts, latency, status codes, and user ID hash. If you need verbatim transcripts for debugging, that can be enabled under strict controls and only for specific sessions with consent — and those are treated as PII and subject to retention rules.

[04:28] Priya Nair: Next KMS discussion — do you offer BYOK and HSM-backed keys? We have a policy that keys should remain in our control.
[04:36] Derek Salazar: We provide customer-managed keys via supported cloud KMS integrations (AWS KMS, GCP CMEK, Azure Key Vault) and HSM-backed key options for Private deployments. For Hosted we offer envelope encryption where customer key wraps the data key. For Private deployments you can run a local HSM. We also support key rotation and audit logs for KMS operations.
[05:01] Liam O'Rourke: If we do BYOK, what's the flow for key revocation or rotating without disrupting inference?
[05:08] Derek Salazar: The runtime caches decrypted data keys for performance (KV cache) — during rotation we do rolling rewraps of data keys and drain sessions. We'll walk through the rotation playbook. For high-throughput apps we recommend staged rotation windows.

[05:40] Maya Chen: Back to compliance mapping — Sara, you asked about evidence for auditors. We can provide: SOC 2 mapping matrix, redacted Type II report, ISO control matrix, audit logs export instructions, and screenshots of role assignments. We'll add these to Trust Center and email you with access.
[05:58] Sara Mendoza: Will the Trust Center show per-tenant artifacts or is it corporate? We need per-entity evidence.
[06:04] Derek Salazar: Trust Center is tenant-aware; we can grant read-only access scoped to your account so you see the evidence that pertains to your deployment (reports, control mappings, organizational diagrams).

[06:20] Liam O'Rourke: About network egress — we need to know which external endpoints Redwood calls, IP ranges, and whether customers can block egress.
[06:29] Derek Salazar: We'll share an IP range and FQDN list. For private/VPC you can restrict egress with NAT rules; for Dedicated we can do explicit allow-lists and peering. There's also an option for 'no public egress' in on-prem/private installs. We'll include a sample egress policy in the doc pack.

[07:05] Priya Nair: Any certifications around vulnerability scanning and patching cadence? Patch windows?
[07:12] Maya Chen: We run automated vulnerability scans and a monthly patch cadence for critical infra. For major security patches we do emergency deploys with customer notification. Derek: SLA around patching?
[07:21] Derek Salazar: We follow CVE triage and aim for critical fixes within 72 hours for managed environments; we document all changes in the change log and provide release notes in Trust Center.

[07:40] Speaker 1: (inaudible) sorry, can you repeat the BYOK flow?
[07:44] Derek Salazar: Yeah, the high level is: you create keys in your KMS, grant Redwood's service account an encrypt/decrypt role scoped to key usage, we do envelope encryption with a data key generated per-tenant, and you retain root key control.

[08:10] Sara Mendoza: About ISO 27001: do you provide an auditable control mapping for Annex A? Our auditor wants a table mapping each Annex A control to Redwood artifacts.
[08:20] Derek Salazar: Yes — we provide an ISO control matrix that maps Annex A controls to evidence, including policies, implementation statements, and how responsibilities are split in Dedicated/Private. We'll share that matrix and a sample auditor pack.

[08:40] Liam O'Rourke: One worry: vendor lock-in of logs. We need to ensure easy exports if we ever migrate.
[08:47] Maya Chen: Exportability is part of our design. Logs, metrics, and snapshots can be exported via APIs or routed to your S3/Syslog. We can also provide a one-time evidence dump for audits.

[09:10] Priya Nair: Are there any known gaps between the SOC 2 report and what an ISO auditor will expect?
[09:17] Derek Salazar: They cover similar ground but ISO demands documented management processes (e.g., continual improvement records) and a few Annex A controls that are organizational. We'll show how we map SOC 2 criteria to Annex A items and where you might need customer-side evidence for the private deployment constraints.

[09:45] Maya Chen: On the product side, RBAC roles are templated but customizable. You can set granular permissions like "model-deploy", "billing-view", "audit-log-read". For SAML partners we sync groups into those roles.

[10:05] Liam O'Rourke: For our compliance automation, we use HashiCorp Vault for secrets and AWS KMS as our primary. Can you integrate with those?
[10:12] Derek Salazar: Yes — we support AWS KMS and can integrate for envelope keys. For Vault, we can integrate via a secure connector in Private deployments; for Hosted we usually align with cloud KMS. We'll outline connector options.

[10:35] Maya Chen: One operational note: when you enable private/VPC, some telemetry is still required for health checks; we can minimize telemetry and clearly label what's sent.
[10:45] Priya Nair: What about penetration testing and attack surface reviews? We have a vendor pen test calendar.
[10:52] Derek Salazar: Redwood does annual third-party penetration tests and will share summaries; for Dedicated/Private we support joint-pen tests under a coordination process with our security team. We'll include the pen test policy and how to request scoping.

[11:20] Sara Mendoza: Can we get a sample SOC 2 auditor's request list that maps to artifacts you can supply? That helps our auditor speed through.
[11:28] Maya Chen: Yes — we'll include an auditor checklist that shows which artifacts we provide and which ones are customer-provided.

[11:40] Priya Nair: On data residency — we need EU only for a subset of datasets. Is partial residency supported, like routing EU data to EU-only model instances?
[11:50] Derek Salazar: Yes, we support region pinning per-tenant or per-route. For strict EU-only, we'd recommend a Dedicated or Private deployment provisioned in EU region. For hosted, we can route specific projects to EU regions and ensure the storage and compute stay there. We'll outline the architecture for cross-region isolation.

[12:20] Liam O'Rourke: A technical ask — can you surface the audit event schema? We'll map it to our SIEM fields.
[12:27] Derek Salazar: We'll attach the audit schema (JSON) with field descriptions. Note: in some automated transcripts that schema field name becomes 'k v cache' sometimes in docs, but the schema will be correct in the repo.

[12:50] Maya Chen: Okay I want to capture decisions — Priya, you need redacted SOC2 and Trust Center access; Derek will prepare KMS diagram and log export samples; Liam will confirm network constraints; Sara needs auditor checklist. Everyone good?
[13:06] Priya Nair: Yep. A couple of small items: is there a cost delta for extended log retention?
[13:12] Derek Salazar: There is — extended retention and SIEM export are part of the enterprise package or add-on. We'll include pricing in the follow-up.

[13:30] Speaker 2: (crosstalk) also curious about SLAs for availability in dedicated pools.
[13:36] Maya Chen: For Dedicated we offer SLA-backed uptime and predictable latency — we'll include the SLA doc in the follow-up pack.

[13:50] Liam O'Rourke: Any blockers for us to start a pilot next month? We have a pilot window starting 2027-01-10.
[13:58] Maya Chen: Pilot looks doable — next steps: access to Trust Center, whiteboard sessions for VPC design, and a scoped pilot SOW. We'll draft a one-page pilot plan and send.

[14:20] Derek Salazar: I'll add a note about key rotation, BYOK operations, and the rewrap process to the KMS doc. Also include sample Terraform snippets for IAM roles and SCIM group mapping.

[14:40] Priya Nair: Last question — do you provide chain-of-custody for evidence delivery to auditors?
[14:46] Derek Salazar: Yes — we can provide timestamps, checksums, and access logs for any exported artifacts, and put those exports behind a limited expiry link.

[15:00] Maya Chen: Alright, we'll follow up with the packet. Thanks everyone for the good discussion. Any final Qs?
[15:06] Sara Mendoza: No, that's it. Thanks.
[15:09] Priya Nair: Thanks all.
[15:12] Liam O'Rourke: Appreciate it.

[15:20] Meeting end. Recording stopped.
